text: Every morning, one crore sixty-four lakh Paytm Soundboxes say the same words. Money received. But not one of them tells a shopkeeper what's coming.
Meet Murugan. He runs a small store in Velachery, Chennai. He sells eleven thousand rupees a day. And still, on the day he needs it most, the money isn't there.

His Pongal stock is due on the sixth of January. Eighty thousand rupees. At today's pace, he'll be thirty-two thousand short. He's not alone: only fourteen percent of small businesses ever reach formal credit.
So we built Kaasu. Tamil for money. It lives on the Soundbox already on his counter, and in the Paytm app he already uses.

Fifty-three days before Pongal, his Soundbox speaks to him, in Tamil. Save six hundred a day. Collect what customers owe. Borrow only the gap. He says yes. He confirms with his PIN. Money never moves on voice alone.
Udhaar reminders come from Paytm, not from him, so no regular feels insulted. Floods pause his loan. Customers pre-book their Pongal hampers. And his loan shrinks from thirty-five thousand to eleven.
It runs on what Paytm already has. The Soundbox fleet, UPI, and regulated partners who hold the money and lend, built to RBI's rules.
Nobody else answers, acts, brings money in, and plans ahead. At ten lakh shops, that's around a hundred and thirty crore rupees a year for Paytm.
On the sixth of January, the distributor's truck arrives. Murugan pays in full. And his Soundbox says: Pongal stock paid. Happy Pongal, Murugan. Kaasu. Every shop's cash, planned.
